corner.topic: Relative strength: what the RS line against the S&P 500 tells you before the price does
corner.headline: The RS Line Gets To New Ground Before The Price Does
corner.deck: Apple's relative strength line hit a new high Friday while the stock sat 1.3% below its peak, and that is the order a leader shows it in.
body: The relative strength line divides a stock's price by the S&P 500 and plots the result. When it rises, the stock is beating the market. When it falls, the stock is lagging, even if the price is going up. The line has nothing to do with a rating or a rank. It is a ratio you can draw yourself, and it answers one question: is this stock doing better than the index it is measured against?

The rule is about the order things happen in. In O'Neil's work the best leaders show the RS line at a new high before the price breaks out, or at least on the same day. A line that is already at new high ground while the stock still sits in its base or just under its old peak means money is favoring the stock over everything else while it rests. When price is at a new high but the line is not, the stock is rising with the tide instead of beating it.

Apple shows the first case on Friday's chart. The stock closed at 356.27, up 0.4%, 1.3% below its 52-week high of 360.83. The RS line closed at a new high. The line is at its peak and the price is not. It came on a day the S&P 500 fell 0.4% and closed 1.4% under its 50-day line: Apple rose while the index slipped.

The rest of the chart supports it. Apple broke out of a four-week flat base on Oct. 22 past a 345.44 buy point, trading 1.17x average volume that day. The base was 5.7% deep. Sixteen sessions later the stock is 3.1% past the buy point and inside a range that runs to 362.71. It sits 2.9% above its 21-day line and 5.1% above its 50-day line, and it closed 1.15 ATRs from the 21-day line. That is a trend that is not stretched.

Now the contrast. Costco broke out Friday from a 25-week cup and hit a 52-week high of 1,109.50 in the session. Its RS line is 6.9% below its own high. The price got to new ground and the line did not. That is not a reason to call the breakout bad, but it is a weaker profile than Apple's, and it is the kind of gap a reader should know is there.

AMD shows the third case. It holds an RS rank of 99 of 99 on the desk's list on the strength of a 149.4% gain this year. Its RS line is 15.0% below its high, and Friday the stock fell 8.8% and closed under its 50-day line. A high rank built on past months can hide a line that has already rolled over. The line shows what is happening now; the rank shows what already happened.

Without the line, Apple, Costco and AMD would read as three big stocks near or recently near their highs. With it, they split apart: one leading the market, one keeping pace with it, one losing ground to it.
takeaways: The RS line is the stock divided by the S&P 500; it rises only when the stock beats the index.
The strongest setups show the RS line at a new high before or with the price breakout, as Apple's does now.
A new price high with a lagging RS line, as on Costco's breakout, means the stock is keeping pace, not leading.
A high RS rank can hide a falling line; AMD ranks 99 with its line 15.0% off its high.
Check the line during a weak tape: a line that climbs while the index falls marks the stock to watch.

chief.verdict: The leadership has shrunk to defensive and old-economy names: Costco, Apple, Grainger and ConocoPhillips hold their bases while the AI chips crack, with AMD down 8.8% on 1.86 times normal volume and only 21% of the ai chips group above its 50-day line. Healthcare (88% above the 50-day) and megacaps (75%) are where the money is hiding, and that is a sign of caution, not of risk-taking. The Nasdaq sits 4.6% under its 50-day and right on its 200-day (-0.0%), so the risk leans down until that line holds.
